title: Implement topological sorting of a directed acyclic graph using depth-first search, producing the order by reversing the post-order of the DFS.
keyPoints: DFS topological sort pushes a node onto a stack after all its descendants are fully explored (post-order).
Reversing the post-order stack yields a valid topological ordering.
Use three colors (white, gray, black) to track node states and detect cycles via back edges.
A gray node encountered during recursion indicates a back edge and therefore a cycle.
Time is O(V + E) and space is O(V) for the recursion stack and state array.
For very deep graphs, convert the recursion to an explicit stack to avoid stack overflow.

s1_definition.oneliner: DFS each node, push it after its descendants finish (post-order), then reverse the post-order to get the topological sort; use three colors to catch cycles.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **DFS from each unvisited node** – explore all reachable descendants before recording a node.
- **Post-order recording** – push a node onto a stack only after all its descendants are fully explored.
- **Reverse to get order** – the reversed stack is a valid topological order.
- **Three-color cycle detection** – white (unvisited), gray (in progress), black (finished); a gray-to-gray edge is a cycle.
- **O(V + E) time** – each node and edge is visited once.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of resolving dependency chains for report generation at National Bank of India. Pankaj dives down each dependency chain to its deepest point, records stages as they finish, and when he reverses that finish order he gets a sequence where every dependency comes before the stage needing it.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  DFS traversal (starting from node 0):

  dfs(0) → color[0]=GRAY
    dfs(1) → color[1]=GRAY
      dfs(3) → color[3]=GRAY
        dfs(4) → color[4]=GRAY
          no successors → color[4]=BLACK, push 4
        color[3]=BLACK, push 3
      color[1]=BLACK, push 1
    dfs(2) → color[2]=GRAY
      dfs(3) → color[3]=BLACK (skip)
      color[2]=BLACK, push 2
    color[0]=BLACK, push 0

  Stack (top to bottom): [0, 2, 1, 3, 4]
  Pop order (topological):  0, 2, 1, 3, 4
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
DFS-based topological sort runs depth-first search from each unvisited node and pushes a node onto a stack only after all of its descendants have been fully explored. Because a node is recorded only after everything it points to, the post-order places each node after its successors, so reversing gives the topological order.

The three-color scheme is essential for cycle detection. White for unvisited, gray for nodes on the current recursion path, and black for finished. A gray-to-gray edge is a back edge forming a cycle. The gray versus black distinction prevents false positives from cross edges.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, a report-generation pipeline had stages depending on upstream stages, and they had to run in dependency order. DFS post-order produced that order by finishing each stage's dependencies before recording it.

For very deep graphs I convert the recursion to an explicit stack to avoid overflow, or I use Kahn's algorithm which is naturally iterative.

Remember one sentence: DFS finishes descendants first, so reversing the post-order gives the topological order, and three colors detect cycles.
